title: Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, Religious
short_summary: Elizabeth of Hungary (1207-1231) was a royal princess and landgravine of Thuringia who devoted her wealth and personal labor to the poor and sick. Widowed at twenty, she founded a hospital at Marburg and spent the last years of her brief life in prayer and service under Franciscan influence.
key_facts: Her memorial is celebrated on November 17.
She was born in 1207, a daughter of King Andrew II of Hungary.
She married Ludwig IV of Thuringia and had three children.
After Ludwig's death, she founded a hospital at Marburg and died there in 1231 at age twenty-four.

sections.heading: A Hungarian princess in Thuringia
sections.body: Elizabeth was sent as a child from the Hungarian court to be raised in Thuringia for a dynastic marriage. She married Ludwig IV in 1221. Contemporary testimony describes an affectionate marriage and a young ruler whose religious life included direct service to the poor, distribution of food and clothing, and care for people with illnesses that others feared to approach.

sections.heading: Famine and works of mercy
sections.body: During a severe famine in 1226, while Ludwig was away, Elizabeth opened stores of grain and expanded relief for the population. She supported a hospital near the Wartburg and personally tended patients. Her conduct could alarm members of the court, but Ludwig defended her charitable use of their resources.

sections.heading: Widowhood
sections.body: Ludwig died of disease in 1227 while traveling to join a crusade. Elizabeth, then about twenty, faced conflict over her income and residence. A settlement eventually provided for her support. At Marburg she established a hospital dedicated to Saint Francis, adopted a plain habit, and organized her life around prayer and care of the sick.

sections.heading: Death and memory
sections.body: Elizabeth died on November 17, 1231. Reports of holiness and miracles spread rapidly, and Pope Gregory IX canonized her in 1235. She became a patron of hospitals, charitable organizations, nurses, widows, and members of the Secular Franciscan tradition. The rose miracle familiar in later art is a beloved legend rather than an episode found in the earliest testimony.

catholic_connection_sections.heading: Charity face to face
catholic_connection_sections.body: Elizabeth gave money and food, but she also crossed the distance between a court and a hospital ward. Her holiness took visible form in sustained personal contact with people who were poor or ill.

catholic_connection_sections.heading: Holiness in marriage and widowhood
catholic_connection_sections.body: Her life includes years as wife, mother, public figure, and widow. The Church remembers all of these as places where Christian vocation can mature.

historical_cautions: The miracle in which bread hidden in Elizabeth's cloak becomes roses appears in later tradition and should be identified as legend.
Descriptions of her spiritual director Conrad of Marburg and of family conflict require care because the sources reflect competing interests.
